ops.markdown:
Grounding is auditable because **you drew the boundary**. You uploaded the documents, so you can ask for something you know is absent and watch whether the tool refuses. That negative test is what proves the fence exists.

Web grounding removes the boundary. Perplexity's knowledge base is the live web — nothing is knowably absent, so there is no negative test to run. The fence is still there; the ability to audit it is gone.

So the question moves up a layer: not *is the tool correct*, but **how do we grade the citations it hands us**.

Why instinct is not enough: web-grounded output arrives looking settled. Real URLs, real articles, really containing the claim. Nothing in the presentation separates a good source from a worthless one, so there is no seam for skepticism to catch on. It needs explicit checks, run one at a time.

Five tools in scope — ChatGPT, Gemini Notebook, Perplexity, Claude, Google AI Studio. Claude is the only one new to the course.

ops.title: What changes when you stop owning the knowledge base

ops.label: You don't — the web is the knowledge base
Ask for something you know is absent
ops.detail: The negative test. It only works because you know what is not in there.

ops.label: It refuses, or it is hallucinating
The live web chose the documents
Nothing is knowably absent
ops.detail: No negative test can be constructed, and you cannot know what the correct retrieval would have been.

ops.label: You get an answer with citations attached

cells.result: No answer — cannot answer a current event from that configuration

cells.config: Its usual KB — three files on prompt stack, hallucination, defensive prompting
cells.result: No answer — the sources contain nothing on the subject

cells.config: Web search always on, cannot be turned off
cells.result: An answer — a strike dated 29-30 July 2026, news articles attached

ops.title: Two refusals are not the same refusal

ops.label: "Between USA and Iran, what was the last strike?"
ops.detail: Deliberately broken wording. He says so at the time; §5 shows it was the cause of the failure.

ops.label: Lacked the reach
ops.detail: A current event past the cutoff, with no mechanism to go further. Give it the reach and it answers — nothing about the tool was wrong for the job.

ops.label: Gemini Notebook on three prompting files
Wrong tool by remit
ops.detail: Its job is answering from your sources, and this is not in them. It could have had live access and still correctly declined. This is the grounding fence working — the negative test, run by accident.

ops.label: Both print "no answer"
ops.detail: One is a capability limit, the other is correct behaviour. Identical on screen — which is why reading the output alone tells you very little.

ops.markdown:
Asked whether they would accept Perplexity's answer, the class says yes. Citations attached, a specific date, articles you can click. It looks legitimate.

That unanimous acceptance is what the rest of the lecture dismantles — and the class was not being careless. **There was nothing visible to object to.**

This is the hinge: if a confident, cited, on-topic answer can still be wrong, the check has to run on the sources, not on the answer.

ops.label: A citation certifies provenance, not judgement
Test: how fast does the answer to my question change?
ops.detail: Old is a relationship between the article's date and the question's time-sensitivity, not a property of the article. A property of your question, not of the source.

ops.label: A 2008 paper on the Harappan civilization is not old
ops.detail: Nothing about the subject has moved. For the US-Iran question, three to five months back is useless — you want days, or a couple of weeks.

ops.label: Test: who is accountable for being right about this?
Authority means remit, not size or fame
ops.detail: NASA for the Earth-Moon distance, because its entire job is that subject. Government sites for a question about policy. The question is whether the publisher is accountable for being right about this specific thing.

ops.label: Forums rank by popularity, not verification
ops.detail: An incorrect answer with five upvotes becomes the topmost answer — which is exactly what a crawler picks up. This is the glue-on-pizza case told mechanically.

ops.label: Wikipedia: not fully
ops.detail: Solid for public, well-known knowledge; riskier for niche topics, because anyone can edit and reviewers miss things.

ops.label: Test: is anyone else saying it?
ops.detail: One outlet carries the claim while the others either contradict it or are silent.

ops.markdown:
In 2024 Google's AI Overview told people to add glue to their pizza so the cheese would stick. The source was a years-old Reddit joke — someone complained their cheese was slipping, someone else joked about glue.

**Nothing hallucinated.** No invented source, no misquote, no blending. It retrieved a real post from a real thread and reported it faithfully. Every step of the pipeline worked.

The citation was genuine. The source was worthless.

Retrieval quality and source quality are separate problems. A perfectly functioning retrieval system will confidently serve you garbage if garbage is what it found.

ops.label: News is reliable because it is liable
ops.detail: Publish a false statement of fact and you can be sued, and made to justify your sources. The accountability is what produces the accuracy — which also predicts where the accuracy stops.

ops.label: An unverified claim you want to run
Put it in the headline as a question
ops.detail: "Has X happened?" is not an assertion of fact, so there is nothing to sue over. The claim reaches the reader; the liability does not attach.

ops.label: A deniable headline becomes a sourced claim
ops.detail: The punctuation carries the entire legal and epistemic weight of the sentence, and it does not survive retrieval.

ops.question: He says uncorroborated means the information is incorrect — but the quiz insists absence of citations means unverified, not false. Which does an uncorroborated claim get?

ops.label: Recency — when was this published?
ops.detail: Runs first, and it overrides. Match the source's time window to the window the question asks about — which is sometimes all of history.

ops.label: The question's tense sets the window
ops.detail: "Who is PM" wants today. "Who was PM" wants the full list or the most recent — a partial list from the middle is itself a recency failure, however good the articles behind it. Recency is not "prefer new".

ops.label: Corroboration — do others agree?
ops.detail: You want the information available widely rather than resting on a single voice. His three-friends analogy — two accounts agree, one does not — he labels naive himself.

ops.label: Relevance — does it answer THIS question?
ops.detail: The subtle one. Not an off-topic article, which you would catch instantly — a recent, authoritative, corroborated, genuinely excellent source answering a different question. Every quality signal fires and it still does the wrong job.

ops.label: Trustworthy — only if all four pass
Verify before acting
ops.detail: A failed check means unverified, not false. You go and check before you act on it.

ops.markdown:
Ask who the Prime Minister of India is. Get an answer naming a PM from 2003, supported by ten genuine news articles from 2003.

Run the other three checks. **Authority** — real news organisations, passes. **Relevance** — directly on the question of who the PM is, passes. **Corroboration** — ten sources all agreeing, passes hardest of all, because contemporaneous reports of the same true fact always agree.

And the answer is wrong.

The articles are not even wrong. They were accurate when published. There is no bad source anywhere in the chain — nothing the other three checks could catch.

That is what *percolates down* means: a recency failure is not outvoted three to one. It invalidates the other three passes, because those checks were run against sources answering a question about 2003.

Which is why recency runs **first** rather than just counting for more. Verifying the credentials of a stale source is careful work on an answer to a question nobody asked.

ops.label: Test: is anyone else saying it?
ops.detail: One outlet carries the claim while the others either contradict it or are silent. Settled: a failed check means unverified, not false — the framework's endpoint says verify before acting. His stronger phrasing, that an uncorroborated claim is therefore incorrect, overshoots his own diagram.

ops.title: The prompt decided which sources you were ever shown

ops.label: "Last strike" is how headlines describe a completed, named event
ops.detail: The phrase has its own life on the web. Retrieval optimised for documents matching it.

ops.label: The older, well-covered strike
ops.detail: Every outlet had written it up as THE strike. The newer incident was ambiguous and unattributed, so nobody described it that way — recent, but not matching the phrase.

ops.label: All four checks pass on the wrong answer
ops.detail: Authoritative outlets, heavily corroborated, directly relevant to "the last strike", recent enough. The framework grades the sources you got; this failure happened one step earlier.

ops.label: "the MOST RECENT strike with respect to the US-Iran war"
The newer incident, immediately
ops.detail: Same tool, same web, same moment. Different phrase. The correct answer had been inside the citation set all along — the summary skipped past it. Demo output from a live tool, not a verified fact.

ops.label: Perplexity read 15 articles and did the retrieval well
ops.detail: "Perplexity is not a bad player in this." It optimised for exactly what it was given.

ops.label: Prompt-side: a restrictive prompt or the wrong terminology
ops.detail: Recency gets tampered with before you ever see a citation. This is the first line of defence — write it into the prompt: prioritise recency, sources should be corroborated, sources should carry authority.

ops.label: Source-side: the citations themselves may be old
ops.detail: Good prompt, good answer, stale sources. This is where you step back and run the four checks — the second line of defence, not the first.

ops.label: Move the framework upstream
ops.detail: From something applied to the output to something that shapes the retrieval.

cells.why: Official scientific body, publishing on its own site, current

cells.src: A forum post arguing climate sensitivity is far higher than IPCC estimates
cells.why: Recent, but a single social-media post — no peer review, no methodology, does not cite the study it invokes, author's credibility cannot be established

cells.src: A 2021 advocacy blog arguing warming is not human-caused
cells.why: Old and never updated, not peer-reviewed, no scientific grounding — a position promoted without standard review or transparency

ops.markdown:
On the middle source: **"reading this will make you feel that this is absolutely correct, but it is not."**

Recent, articulate, arguing a technical claim with apparent rigour. Fluency and confidence are not signals of anything.

Same lesson as glue on pizza, arriving from the opposite direction. There, a joke was retrieved faithfully. Here, an assertion is written persuasively. Both defeat a reader who is judging how it reads.

---

This is **not** a rule about excluding sources from your search. All three can and will surface, and you may want to know the argument exists.

The rule is about what reaches your **output**: such citations should not be included when you share the result with an end user or a client.

ops.title: Why not just show both sides?

ops.markdown:
A student proposes returning citations for and against a claim and letting the reader judge.

His answer is a product argument, not an epistemics one: *"the expectation from an end user is pretty lazy — they want to be fed information directly. If they have to go and read the article, then they would not come to you."*

The tool answers with confidence even when it is wrong, so the fix belongs in the prompt, not in the user's lap.

ops.title: Perplexity never tells you what it searched

ops.markdown:
A source-ranking problem — exactly the one that just happened — is possible and completely invisible.

He could only diagnose this case because he happened to open the other articles himself.

That gap is what Google AI Studio closes.

ops.question: Moving the checks into the prompt means the disconfirming sources are dropped before the reader ever sees them. Does that make the output more trustworthy, or only more confident?

ops.title: Grounded vs ungrounded, and what a citation is

ops.markdown:
**Ungrounded is describing a dream.** "It is not real. It's just my brain using its thoughts."

**Grounded is teaching the class.** Scaler's context, his own academia, articles he has read, his own research — all external, all checkable.

**A citation** is the article or URL a piece of generated text was built from. Nothing more than that.

---

The pairing works because a dream is not a lie. Dreams contain plenty of true material, recombined. What a dream lacks is anything outside itself to check against — and the grounded side is a list of external things.

So the distinction is not truth against falsehood. It is **traceable against untraceable**. Grounding does not buy correctness; it buys a chain you can follow back, which is what makes correctness checkable at all. A grounded answer built on stale articles was still wrong, and a model answering from training sometimes has the right answer sitting in its weights.

**Unverified is not false.** He hedges deliberately — answering from memory *could be* ungrounded, and ungrounded has *more potential* of hallucination. The framework's endpoint says the same thing (one failure means verify before acting), and so does the quiz. Three places in one lecture land on that line.

ops.title: Claude web search — and how to tell whether it ran

ops.label: Web search: toggled on or off per conversation
It CAN call a search mid-conversation when grounding is needed
ops.detail: The decision is made during the conversation, per turn, by the model. ChatGPT's search is a mode you set; Perplexity's is always on; Notebook has no web reach into a grounded answer. Claude's is a judgement call.

ops.label: "Can" means may or may not
ops.detail: His whiteboard annotates that exact phrase in his own hand. The danger is not that it fails to search — it is that you assume it searched when it did not. A confident, plausible answer looks identical either way.

ops.label: Check for citation markers and a source tab
Grounded — now run the four checks
Both absent — unverified, treat as ungrounded
ops.detail: Not a quality check. It does not say the sources were good — it says which regime you are in: gradeable, or not yet gradeable. The prior question to the framework.

ops.label: School, college, your own projects — known
ops.detail: You do not search the internet to know how to eat, or run, or write about a familiar subject.

ops.label: A new company's products and rules — not known
Go and learn it, using what you already know
Anything past the cutoff — not known
Fetch articles, then read them with what it already knows
ops.detail: Retrieval supplies material; comprehension stays the model's own. This corrects the common picture of retrieval as the model going and getting the answer — which is why a bad source produces a bad answer with no error anywhere in the machinery.

ops.markdown:
Retrieval is **cyclic, not linear**: decide what to read, fetch, assess whether it is the right document, read, summarise — looping as needed. Not one pass.

And all of it runs on the far side: *"There is no augmentation happening onto your prompt. It's actually happening on Claude's side."* Your request has already left.

That is why the search decision is unauditable from where you sit. It is not that the tool hides it — the whole retrieve-assess-read loop runs somewhere you were never party to. What comes back is the output, plus citation markers if it searched.

The decision rules are a black box too: which searches to trigger, which engine, which sources to prefer. *"That is Claude's secret recipe."* Same gap Perplexity leaves.

**One clarification:** "not using the internet" refers to the model, not to you. *"Do not think that you can turn off your Wi-Fi."* Your request always travels over the internet. What varies is whether the model reaches further out from its end.

ops.label: Grounding with Google Search — under Tools, OFF by default
ops.detail: The trap: run a first query, get a fluent answer with no sources, conclude the tool does not ground — when you never enabled it. Same shape as the stale ChatGPT settings: testing a configuration you do not have.

ops.label: It displays the Google search it actually ran
ops.detail: "Display of search suggestion is required when using grounding with Google Search." Required, not offered — the transparency is a condition of using the tool, which is a firmer basis for trusting it to stay than vendor goodwill. A complex request produces several searches, so you also see how it decomposed the question.

ops.label: Run that query in Google yourself — the top results are the cited sources
ops.detail: You can reproduce the retrieval by hand.

ops.label: The wrong-phrase failure becomes legible
ops.detail: The "last strike" failure was only caught because he happened to open the other articles. With the query visible you see the phrase it searched for, notice it is not the phrase you needed, and fix the prompt. An invisible failure mode becomes a visible one.

ops.markdown:
Chrome DevTools -> Network, filter to Fetch/XHR, inspect the `generateContent` response. Each cited source carries a **confidence score between 0 and 1** — how confident the model is that the source is useful. Roughly 0.75-0.8 is confident, 0.30-0.4 is not.

**His own caveats.** Not usable inside AI Studio's interface at all, and the raw response is "a very botched up place to search for it". It becomes genuinely useful when you call the API from code, where you can drop low-confidence sources before they reach your output. He does not demo the API call — the setup would leave the class unable to reproduce it — and defers it.

**It scores usefulness, not credibility.** It is the model's judgement about whether a document helps answer the question — closest to the *relevance* check, and not authority, recency or corroboration. A recent, well-written, entirely unaccountable post that directly addresses your question can score high.

So it does not replace the four checks. It is an automatable filter to run **before** them, at scale, in code.

**Warning:** the request payload in that same network tab contains the API key. Worth knowing before you share a DevTools panel.

cells.see: The sources, when it searched. Not the decision to search, not the search itself.
The search query, the sources, and a per-source confidence score.
More visibility, further from an end user — which is why AI Studio should never be put in front of a client

ops.title: Three misconceptions about a missing citation

ops.markdown:
**"It's grounded, it just hides citations sometimes."** Never. If it searched, it shows the citations. The signal is reliable — which is the whole basis of the detection rule.

**"It never needs to search for factual questions like this."** Not true. A question needing recent information should trigger a search. *Factual* does not mean *static*.

**"No citation means the information is definitely wrong."** Also not true. Sometimes the training data holds the correct answer.

---

The third cuts both ways, which is why it needs saying. **Absence of citations means unverified, not false.** The point of the detection rule is not to reject uncited answers — it is to know you have not checked one yet.

---

**In practice, corroboration is never reached.** Working a quiz case he eliminates in order: authority cannot be judged from the description, relevance plainly passes, and corroboration is not reached yet — *"we are first asking whether it is even correct to pick this article or not."* You do not corroborate a source you have not cleared for recency.

**Stale is counterproductive, not merely useless.** An article from March saying a player is perfectly fit cannot justify a claim about his fitness in July; anything could have happened in between. A stale source does not leave you where you started — it leaves you worse off, holding a confident belief sourced to a real article, having stopped looking. Absence of information makes you cautious. Stale information makes you certain and wrong.

**And this is the hard one.** That quiz scored 74%, the weakest of the session, against 93-98% on the rest — on the check he spent the most time on. *Recency is relative to the question* is difficult to hold, because every instinct says a good article is a good article. It is the failure where nothing looks wrong.

ops.title: Pick the right tool — five scenarios

cells.scenario: A one-off fact check right now, without leaving the conversation you are already in
cells.why: The chat is general-purpose and multi-topic. Notebook is capped at its uploaded context; Perplexity only does web search so it cannot carry the general task; AI Studio is not built for a non-developer. Claude grounds mid-conversation with no context switch

cells.scenario: A recurring weekly brief, reusable with one click
cells.why: The one tuned for web search and deep, repeatable research

cells.scenario: A 90-minute recording to mine for quotes
cells.why: A single long video needing a timestamped transcript. "Without fail"

cells.scenario: Cross-referencing 12 of your own uploaded reports, fully cited
cells.why: Anything built on documents you supply — checking whether a pile of your own material is internally consistent and corroborated

cells.scenario: Building this into your own app, needing to see exactly which search queries ran
cells.why: The only one exposing the search it performed and per-source confidence — the developer path

ops.title: What is actually doing the selecting

ops.label: The grounding surface narrows the field
ops.detail: Documents you supply, the live web, or one piece of media. Three of the five scenarios fall straight out of this and need no further thought.

ops.label: Then the shape of the work decides
Is this a step inside a larger task?
ops.detail: Scenario 1's eliminations are all non-grounding reasons. Perplexity would answer the fact perfectly well — it is rejected because the fact check sits inside something else and Perplexity cannot hold the something else. The winner is chosen on context-switching cost.

ops.label: Will it be run repeatedly?
ops.detail: "Reusable with one click" is why scenario 2 is Perplexity saved as a Space rather than just Perplexity.

ops.label: Who reads the output?
ops.detail: The same axis as the visibility ladder. The developer path gets the most visible tool precisely because a developer is reading it — and AI Studio should not go in front of a client.

ops.label: A selection procedure, not a feature comparison

cells.scenario: A 90-minute recording to mine for quotes
cells.why: A single long video needing a timestamped transcript. "Without fail" — though NoteGPT was not taught in this lecture, it appears only in this exercise, so the recommendation carries no new argument behind it

cells.when: Used here mainly to demonstrate the ungrounded state

cells.usp: Behaves as a subject-matter expert; refuses outside its sources
cells.when: Cross-referencing your own documents, fully cited

cells.usp: Cannot turn search off; goes deep across many articles
cells.when: Deep, repeatable research and weekly briefs

cells.usp: Decides during a conversation whether grounding is needed
cells.when: General-purpose work needing a grounded fact partway through

Assembled across the lecture, not delivered as a block

ops.markdown:
The closest pair in the set — both ground in the live web, both cite.

**Claude** is for general-purpose work where grounding is one step among several. Ask it to write a Python script that pulls the third column out of a spreadsheet — no internet needed, it knows how. Then ask it to corroborate the news articles sitting in that column — now it needs the internet, and it goes mid-task.

> "Claude will be able to work for a general purpose task where you might need internet somewhere in the middle, you might not need it, but it will use it when it's needed."

**Perplexity** is for deep research — many articles, summarised, in depth on one topic.

So the split is not about who searches better. It is **whether searching is the task or a step inside the task** — the same scope axis that decided the five scenarios. Hard to separate on capability, trivial to separate on shape of work.

columns.label: What it does when you have touched nothing

cells.risk: Disabling it is the deliberate act — and the setting can silently fail to take effect until a hard refresh

cells.default: Never reaches the web inside a grounded answer
cells.risk: None here — it offers, and will not do it silently
No default to get wrong — and no ungrounded comparison available either

cells.default: Toggleable, and even switched on the model decides per turn
cells.risk: The only tool where correctly configured still does not tell you what happened — hence the detection rule
The reverse of everyone's assumption about a Google developer tool — get it wrong and you conclude it does not ground

ops.title: Every configuration mistake came from a default

ops.markdown:
Not one of them came from a limitation.

Three of the five have a default that surprises. And the two most dangerous are not the least capable — they are **Claude** (configured on, still may not search) and **AI Studio** (the best transparency in the set, silently not grounding).

The failure is not the tool being weak. It is you being confident about a state you never verified.

ops.title: Prompt-level defence is not access control

ops.label: You share a Gem with a defensive prompt over its documents
The person you shared with can open the documents directly
ops.detail: His answer: a genuine limitation of Gems. He believes there may be a setting for hiding them but would not confirm it live and took it to Discord — so it stays open.

ops.label: Or feeds the document to another model and reads it out
ops.detail: A student's follow-up, making the same point from another angle.

ops.label: A defensive prompt governs what the model says, not what the reader can reach
ops.detail: It is an instruction to one model about one conversation. It is not access control. If the document is reachable it is readable — through the interface, through download, through another model. A defence written at the wrong layer is not a weak defence, it is not a defence.

ops.label: Standing guidance: do not put secrets in a document attached to a shared Gem

ops.title: Regional scope is a retrieval-scope failure

ops.markdown:
A gardening notebook built from a video aimed at a foreign audience could not answer a question about plants for Delhi. It offered Northern California instead, because that is what its source covered.

**Nothing malfunctioned.** The knowledge base did not contain the answer and the tool did what a grounded tool should.

So the fix follows from the diagnosis: **add a broader or region-appropriate document.** You cannot prompt your way out of a source that does not cover your case.

Same lesson as the shared-Gem problem, from the other side — fix things at the layer they are broken at.

ops.title: When a grounded tool misbehaves, the cause may not be your documents

ops.label: Check which layer the behaviour came from
Defensive prompting has a balance point
ops.detail: Early submissions were so strong and stringent they stopped answering at all; later ones lowered the guard enough to still answer. A direct request for secrets gets firewalled, while creative phrasing may still extract more than intended.

ops.label: System prompts control verbosity and repetition, not just safety
ops.detail: One Gem answered only about its author's job tooling and kept restating the same points, padding length without adding content. Fixable from the system prompt and the KB documents — steer it to elaborate rather than repeat, in fewer tokens.

ops.label: A refusal can come from the model's own guardrails
ops.detail: A mental-health notebook declined to promise it could fix childhood trauma, then gave the substantive material anyway. Attributed to the underlying LLM, not to anything uploaded.

ops.label: One project per client
ops.detail: Asked what mistake he would avoid if starting over: keep one client's material to one Claude Project. Mixing a second client's material into the same project is "a blunder".
